analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off the West Coast.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently ban offshore oil and gas drilling off California, Oregon, and Washington was referred to the Senate Energy Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing a lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in federal waters off California, Oregon, or Washington. Senator Barbara Boxer introduced it in October 2015 with five Democratic cosponsors from the three West Coast states. It went straight to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and sat there without any action until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and coastal communities of California, Oregon, and Washington would gain permanent legal protection against new offshore drilling platforms and the oil spills they can bring. The West Coast's fishing, tourism, and recreation economies, which depend on clean water and healthy beaches, would be shielded from the risk of a drilling disaster like the ones that have hit other coastlines.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal residents, fisheries, and tourism

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in the outer Continental Shelf off California, Oregon, or Washington, making the ban law rather than a policy that a future administration could reverse.

Because the prohibition is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and overrides other provisions, it would give West Coast states lasting protection for their shorelines, fishing grounds, and coastal economies against the spill risk that comes with offshore drilling.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would permanently lose the ability to lease and drill in Pacific federal waters off the three states, and the federal Treasury would forgo whatever royalties future Pacific drilling might have generated. Consumers would in principle forgo a small slice of future domestic energy supply, though no drilling was planned in those waters under the leasing plans then in effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Pacific leases

drawbacks.text: A permanent statutory ban forecloses domestic oil and gas production in Pacific federal waters along with the federal royalty revenue and energy supply it could have produced, and it removes the case-by-case judgment that the regular five-year leasing process allows.

The bill's practical effect in the short term was limited: under the leasing plans then in effect, no new drilling was scheduled off the West Coast, so the main result would have been locking in protection against a future administration's decisions rather than stopping any current activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a small amount of foregone future energy production and royalties for permanent protection of a long coastline against oil spills, a low-probability but very high-damage risk. Since no Pacific leases were pending, the immediate cost was largely to the oil and gas industry's future options rather than to today's consumers. The main design weakness is that a permanent statutory ban, unlike the routine five-year planning process, allows no room for future reassessment if circumstances change.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer of California introduced the bill on October 7, 2015, joined by five Democratic cosponsors from Washington, Oregon, and California.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept open the possibility of future Pacific drilling, and the Republican-run Energy Committee avoided ever having to vote on a permanent drilling ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that want Pacific access

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban offshore oil and gas leasing off California, Oregon, and Washington.

for.name: 5 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all five represented the three West Coast states the bill would protect.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-majority Energy Committee never took the bill up; it never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently locked the industry out of oil and gas leasing in Pacific federal waters off California, Oregon, and Washington, taking away any future option to drill there. Its interest in keeping those waters open ran against the coastal protection the bill offered residents.

industries.industry: West Coast commercial fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: These industries depend on unpolluted coastal waters and beaches, and a permanent drilling ban would protect them from the spill risk and infrastructure that offshore drilling brings. Their gain tracks directly with what coastal residents want.
